title: Omani Slave Coast
capsule: Omani dominance over the East African coast reached its apogee under Said bin Sultan (r. 1806–1856), who relocated his capital from Muscat to Zanzibar by 1840 and transformed the island into the commercial and administrative center of a maritime empire stretching from the Horn of Africa to Mozambique. Under his direction, clove plantation agriculture was introduced on Zanzibar and Pemba, and caravan networks channeled ivory and enslaved persons from the deep interior to coastal markets; tens of thousands of captives were exported annually, making Zanzibar the largest slave market in the Indian Ocean world. Said signed commercial treaties with the United States (1833), Britain (1839), and France (1844), integrating the coast into global trade. At his death in 1856 the empire was partitioned by British arbitration between his sons Majid (Zanzibar) and Thuwain (Oman).
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The spatial extent of Omani coastal control is moderately attested through treaty records and European consular dispatches, but suzerainty over inland areas and exact southern limits remain imprecise.
